Overview

AOD-9604 is a synthetic peptide based on the C-terminal lipolytic fragment of human growth hormone (residues 176-191, with an added tyrosine). It was developed as an anti-obesity agent intended to stimulate fat metabolism without growth hormone's effects on IGF-1 or blood sugar. It received FDA 'Generally Recognized As Safe' (GRAS) status as a food ingredient but is not FDA-approved as a drug, and its pivotal human obesity trials did not meet their primary weight-loss endpoint.

AOD-9604 (Tyr-hGH Frag 176-191) is a modified C-terminal fragment of human growth hormone, developed at Monash University in Australia. In obese-mouse models it increased fat oxidation and reduced body-weight gain without affecting IGF-1, blood glucose, or tissue growth, with effects linked in part to beta-3 adrenergic receptor signaling. It was advanced as an anti-obesity drug candidate but did not demonstrate significant weight loss versus placebo at the primary endpoint in human trials. It later received FDA GRAS status as a food/supplement ingredient (a different regulatory category from drug approval). It has appeared in sports-doping contexts. It is among peptides reviewed by the FDA for compounding.

Mechanism of Action

Mimics the lipolytic (fat-metabolizing) activity of the C-terminal region of growth hormone, increasing fat oxidation and lipolysis and reducing new fat formation, reportedly without the IGF-1-mediated or glucose effects of full growth hormone. Animal data implicate beta-3 adrenergic receptor signaling.

Overview

BPC-157 is a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide derived from a partial sequence of a protein found in human gastric juice. It has been studied extensively in rodent models for tissue repair, tendon and ligament healing, and gastrointestinal protection. As of 2026 there is essentially no published human clinical efficacy data, and it is not approved by the FDA for any use.

BPC-157 (often called Body Protection Compound-157) is a pentadecapeptide with the sequence GEPPPGKPADDAGLV. It is a stable fragment derived from a protective protein identified in human gastric juice. The large majority of the published research consists of preclinical rodent studies, much of it from a single research group at the University of Zagreb, examining wound, tendon, ligament, muscle, and gastrointestinal healing. Proposed mechanisms center on promotion of angiogenesis, modulation of the nitric oxide pathway, and effects on growth-factor signaling and fibroblast activity. Independent replication of the core findings by unaffiliated laboratories remains limited, and there is a recognized species gap between rodent and human tendon biology. Multiple 2025 systematic and narrative reviews concluded that BPC-157 should be regarded as investigational pending well-designed human trials. A first randomized placebo-controlled human trial in acute hamstring strain was registered in early 2026.

Mechanism of Action

Proposed mechanisms, established primarily in cell and rodent studies, include promotion of angiogenesis and endothelial survival, modulation of the nitric oxide (NO) system, upregulation of growth-factor signaling (including growth hormone receptor expression in tendon fibroblasts), and enhancement of fibroblast migration and extracellular-matrix remodeling. The precise molecular target in humans has not been established.

Overview

Cerebrolysin is not a single peptide but a standardized mixture of low-molecular-weight peptide fragments (~15-25%) and free amino acids (~75-85%) produced by controlled enzymatic hydrolysis of porcine brain protein. It is registered as a medicine in over 40 countries (including Austria, Germany, Russia, and China) for stroke, traumatic brain injury, and dementia, but is not FDA-approved and remains a research-use-only compound in the United States. Its evidence base is unusually large for a peptide product but genuinely mixed: some meta-analyses show benefit, while the largest stroke trial was neutral and a Cochrane review rated dementia evidence as very low quality.

Cerebrolysin (manufactured by EVER Neuro Pharma, Austria, under development code FPF-1070) is produced by standardized enzymatic breakdown of purified porcine brain cortex protein, yielding a defined mixture of peptide fragments below 10,000 daltons plus free amino acids. Its proposed mechanism is neurotrophic-factor mimicry: peptide fragments crossing the blood-brain barrier are reported to interact with Trk receptor signaling (TrkA/TrkB) and resemble the activity of BDNF, NGF, and GDNF, engaging downstream MAPK/ERK and PI3K/Akt pathways involved in neuronal survival, synaptic plasticity, and reduction of glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity. It has an unusually large human trial base for a peptide product -- more than 50 randomized controlled trials across stroke, traumatic brain injury, vascular dementia, and Alzheimer's disease -- but the honest picture is mixed rather than uniformly positive: the largest acute-stroke trial (CASTA, n=1,070) was neutral on its primary endpoint, with only a severe-stroke subgroup showing a trend toward benefit; a 2023 Cochrane review (PMID 37818733) concluded moderate-certainty evidence that Cerebrolysin probably has no effect on all-cause mortality or functional independence after acute ischemic stroke; and a separate Cochrane review of the vascular-dementia evidence rated it 'very low quality' with high risk of bias, noting that nearly all positive trials were funded by the manufacturer. Side-effect rates across trials have consistently been comparable to placebo. It is registered as an approved medicine in more than 40 countries but has never received FDA approval and is not available as a legal prescription product in the United States.

Mechanism of Action

Proposed to act through neurotrophic-factor mimicry: its low-molecular-weight peptide fraction crosses the blood-brain barrier and is reported to interact with Trk receptor signaling (TrkA, TrkB), activating MAPK/ERK and PI3K/Akt pathways involved in neuronal survival, synaptic plasticity, and neurogenesis, resembling the activity of endogenous BDNF, NGF, and GDNF. Also proposed to modulate glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity and support protein-clearance pathways. As an undefined, multi-component mixture rather than a single molecular entity, its pharmacology is inherently harder to characterize than a synthetic peptide.

Overview

CJC-1295 (no DAC), also called Modified GRF (1-29), is a synthetic analog of growth-hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH). It binds the GHRH receptor on the pituitary to stimulate pulsatile GH and IGF-1 release. The 'no DAC' form is short-acting (~30 minutes), which preserves natural pulsatility, in contrast to CJC-1295 with DAC (half-life of several days). It is not FDA-approved and is prohibited in sport.

Native GHRH(1-29) is sermorelin. Modified GRF (1-29) introduces four amino-acid substitutions (positions 2, 8, 15, 27) to resist enzymatic degradation, extending half-life from a few minutes to at least ~30 minutes while keeping the short-acting, pulsatile profile. This is distinct from CJC-1295 'with DAC,' where a Drug Affinity Complex binds albumin to extend half-life to roughly 6-8 days for once-weekly dosing. The no-DAC form is favored in non-clinical use for being more physiologic and easier to titrate, and is commonly paired with a selective GHS such as ipamorelin. It has no approved human therapeutic indication.

Mechanism of Action

Binds the GHRH receptor (GHRHR) on pituitary somatotrophs, activating adenylate cyclase and raising intracellular cAMP, which stimulates synthesis and pulsatile release of growth hormone and downstream IGF-1. The four substitutions confer resistance to dipeptidyl peptidase cleavage.

Overview

CJC-1295 with DAC is a long-acting analog of growth-hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) fragment (1-29), chemically modified with a Drug Affinity Complex (DAC) that covalently binds circulating albumin. This extends its half-life from minutes to approximately 6-8 days, allowing once- or twice-weekly dosing with sustained GH and IGF-1 elevation. It is a distinct entry from CJC-1295 (no DAC) / Modified GRF(1-29), which shares the same peptide backbone but clears in about 30 minutes.

CJC-1295 is built on the same tetrasubstituted GHRH(1-29) backbone as the no-DAC (Modified GRF) version, but carries an added maleimidopropionyl-linked DAC group. After subcutaneous injection, the maleimide reacts with the free thiol on cysteine-34 of circulating albumin, forming a stable covalent thioether bond. Because albumin itself has a plasma half-life of roughly 19 days, this conjugation shields the peptide from renal filtration and proteolytic clearance, extending its own half-life to about 6-8 days. A single dose has been shown in a phase I randomized, placebo-controlled trial (Teichman et al., 2006) to produce dose-dependent 2- to 10-fold GH elevations and 1.5- to 3-fold IGF-1 elevations lasting 9-11 days; with repeated dosing, IGF-1 remained elevated for up to 28 days. It is not FDA-approved and has no approved clinical indication; it is sold as a research chemical.

Mechanism of Action

Binds the GHRH receptor (GHRHR) on pituitary somatotrophs to stimulate GH synthesis and release, identical in principle to the no-DAC form. The DAC modification covalently conjugates the peptide to serum albumin via cysteine-34, adopting albumin's slow clearance kinetics and converting a normally pulsatile, short-acting GHRH signal into a sustained, days-long elevation of GH and downstream IGF-1.

Overview

Dihexa is a small-molecule peptide derivative of angiotensin IV, developed at Washington State University as a potentiator of hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) signaling through the c-Met receptor, reported to drive synaptogenesis at extremely low concentrations in preclinical assays. It has zero completed human clinical trials, and its two foundational research papers have serious, disclosed integrity issues: one carries a formal Expression of Concern and the other was retracted in 2025. It is not FDA-approved.

Dihexa (N-hexanoic-Tyr-Ile-(6) aminohexanoic amide, development code PNB-0408) is a metabolically stabilized peptidomimetic derived from angiotensin IV, designed to act as an allosteric potentiator of HGF binding to its c-Met receptor rather than a direct receptor agonist. The original in vitro synaptogenesis assays (McCoy et al. 2013; Benoist et al. 2014, both from the same Washington State University research group) reported activity at picomolar concentrations, described in secondary sources as many orders of magnitude more potent than BDNF at the same in vitro endpoint -- a claim that reflects a narrow molar comparison at one assay endpoint, not a validated measure of clinical potency. This evidence base has a major integrity caveat: the McCoy 2013 paper carries a published Expression of Concern, and the Benoist 2014 follow-up paper was formally retracted in 2025. An independent 2021 replication by an unrelated group (Sun et al.) provides some supporting evidence from outside the original lab, but Dihexa has no completed human clinical trials. A related compound advancing the same HGF/c-Met mechanism into clinical development, fosgonimeton (ATH-1017), has completed phase 1 human pharmacokinetic and safety studies -- this is a distinct, separately-developed molecule and its human data should not be read as clinical validation of dihexa itself.

Mechanism of Action

Reported to act as an allosteric potentiator of hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) binding to its receptor tyrosine kinase, c-Met, amplifying endogenous HGF signaling rather than acting as a direct agonist. In preclinical models this HGF/c-Met potentiation is proposed to drive synaptogenesis (new dendritic spine and synapse formation). Reported potency claims versus BDNF derive from a narrow in vitro comparison and should not be read as an indicator of relative clinical effect.

Overview

DSIP (delta sleep-inducing peptide) is a naturally occurring nonapeptide first isolated from the cerebral venous blood of sleeping rabbits, associated with slow-wave (delta) EEG activity. It is found endogenously in human plasma and tissues, with levels correlated to circadian rhythm. Its gene, precursor, and receptor have never been identified, and modern reproducibility of its original sleep-inducing effects is limited. It is not FDA-approved.</br>

DSIP has the sequence Trp-Ala-Gly-Gly-Asp-Ala-Ser-Gly-Glu (WAGGDASGE), isolated and characterized by Schoenenberger and Monnier in 1977 after intraventricular infusion into rabbits produced spindle and delta EEG activity with reduced motor activity. Despite the name, its role as a genuine physiological sleep regulator remains scientifically unresolved -- no gene, precursor protein, or dedicated receptor has been identified in the four decades since its discovery, and a substantial review literature (Graf & Kastin 1984; Kovalzon & Strekalova 2006) treats it as 'a still unresolved riddle.' Beyond sleep, DSIP has been studied preclinically for anticonvulsant activity (potentiating valproate in an epilepsy model), analgesic effects via modulation of enkephalin-opioid receptor interactions, and neuroprotection in models of toxic cerebral edema. It crosses the blood-brain barrier and is also absorbed from the gut. It is sold as a research chemical with no approved human indication.

Mechanism of Action

Mechanism is not well characterized; DSIP has no confirmed dedicated receptor. Proposed activities include modulation of GABAergic and opioid (enkephalin) signaling, effects on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, and correlation with circadian rhythm and stress-hormone regulation. Structural similarity to dermorphin (a mu-opioid agonist) has been noted but DSIP's own receptor pharmacology remains unresolved.

Epitalon is a synthetic tetrapeptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly) developed in Russia as a synthetic analog of epithalamin, a bovine pineal-gland extract. Overview

GHK-Cu is the copper(II) complex of the naturally occurring tripeptide glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine (GHK). It is found endogenously in human plasma, saliva, and urine, with plasma levels declining markedly with age. It is widely used as a topical cosmetic ingredient for skin remodeling and collagen synthesis, where human evidence is strongest; systemic and injectable anti-aging uses are far less validated and not FDA-approved.

GHK was isolated from human plasma by Loren Pickart in 1973 after the observation that plasma from younger donors restored more youthful protein-synthesis behavior in aged liver tissue. The tripeptide (Gly-His-Lys) has a strong affinity for copper(II) and readily forms the GHK-Cu complex. Reported plasma concentrations fall from roughly 200 ng/mL around age 20 to about 80 ng/mL by age 60. The free tripeptide (GHK) has molecular formula C14H24N6O4 and MW ~340.4; the copper complex (GHK-Cu) has formula C14H22CuN6O4 and MW ~403.9. GHK-Cu has the most robust human evidence in topical dermatology and cosmetics, where it is an established ingredient (INCI name Copper Tripeptide-1) studied for collagen and glycosaminoglycan synthesis, skin firmness, and wound repair. Broader systemic claims (neuroprotection, lung repair, anti-cancer gene modulation) derive largely from gene-expression analyses and animal models rather than controlled human trials. As sold for injection by research-chemical vendors, GHK-Cu is unapproved and outside any compliant compounding pathway.

Mechanism of Action

GHK binds copper(II) and is proposed to act as a copper carrier and a signaling molecule that modulates expression of a large number of human genes. Documented activities (largely cell-culture and animal) include stimulation of collagen and glycosaminoglycan synthesis in dermal fibroblasts, promotion of angiogenesis, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, and support of wound closure and tissue remodeling.

Overview

GHRP-6 is the original growth hormone-releasing hexapeptide, developed in 1984 as the first compound shown to stimulate GH release through a mechanism independent of GHRH. It acts as an agonist at the ghrelin receptor (GHS-R1a) and is distinguished from later GHRPs like ipamorelin by pronounced appetite stimulation and modest cortisol/prolactin elevation. It is not FDA-approved.

GHRP-6 (His-D-Trp-Ala-Trp-D-Phe-Lys-NH2) is a synthetic met-enkephalin analog discovered by Cyril Bowers at Tulane University through structure-activity screening of unnatural D-amino-acid-substituted enkephalin derivatives. Its 1984 characterization was a landmark finding, demonstrating a second, GHRH-independent pathway for pituitary GH secretion; this research program directly led to identification of the growth hormone secretagogue receptor (GHS-R1a) in 1996 and discovery of its endogenous ligand, ghrelin, in 1999. GHRP-6 has no opioid receptor activity despite its enkephalin origin. Compared to later-generation GHRPs (GHRP-2, hexarelin, ipamorelin), it produces the strongest appetite-stimulating effect of the class and a broader hormonal footprint, including modest cortisol and prolactin elevation at higher doses. It also binds the CD36 scavenger receptor, which has been explored for cardioprotective and cytoprotective properties distinct from its GH-releasing activity.

Mechanism of Action

Agonist at the growth hormone secretagogue receptor (GHS-R1a, the ghrelin receptor) on pituitary somatotrophs, stimulating GH release through a pathway distinct from and synergistic with GHRH signaling. Also binds the CD36 scavenger receptor. Unlike more selective later-generation GHRPs, it produces meaningful ghrelin-receptor-mediated appetite stimulation and modest ACTH/cortisol and prolactin release at higher doses.

Overview

Glutathione is an endogenous tripeptide (gamma-L-glutamyl-L-cysteinylglycine) and the body's most abundant intracellular antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative damage and supporting detoxification pathways. It is a genuine tripeptide (unlike some other compounds marketed alongside it), sold both as an approved injectable in some countries for specific medical uses and, more commonly in wellness/aesthetic markets, as an unapproved 'skin-brightening' or general antioxidant IV/injectable.

Glutathione (GSH) is synthesized from three amino acids -- glutamate, cysteine, and glycine -- with the reactive thiol (-SH) group on cysteine giving it its central redox function: it directly scavenges reactive oxygen species and serves as a cofactor for glutathione peroxidase and glutathione S-transferase enzymes that neutralize peroxides and conjugate xenobiotics for excretion. Endogenous synthesis and recycling (between reduced GSH and oxidized GSSG) is tightly regulated, and depleted glutathione status is associated with oxidative stress in numerous disease states. Injectable/IV glutathione has legitimate, though narrow, clinical uses in some countries (for example as adjunctive therapy in certain respiratory and hepatic contexts), and it is a documented use in HIV-related care. It is separately, and far more visibly, marketed off-label in aesthetic medicine as a 'whitening injection' for skin-lightening, and in wellness IV clinics for general antioxidant/detox support -- uses that are not FDA-approved and for which large randomized efficacy trials are limited, despite glutathione's antioxidant role in basic biology being well established.

Mechanism of Action

Directly scavenges reactive oxygen and nitrogen species via its reactive cysteine thiol group. Serves as an essential cofactor for glutathione peroxidase (neutralizing hydrogen peroxide and lipid peroxides) and glutathione S-transferase (conjugating and detoxifying electrophilic xenobiotics for excretion). Maintains protein sulfhydryl groups in a reduced state and participates in amino acid transport (gamma-glutamyl cycle). The skin-lightening effect claimed in aesthetic use is proposed to work by shifting melanin synthesis from darker eumelanin toward lighter pheomelanin and inhibiting tyrosinase, though this mechanism is better characterized in vitro than confirmed as a robust clinical effect.

Overview

Somatropin is recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) -- a bioidentical, 191-amino-acid copy of the growth hormone naturally secreted by the anterior pituitary. It is FDA-approved under multiple brand names for a specific list of growth-disorder and deficiency indications, and separately (as Serostim) for HIV-associated wasting. Unlike the GH secretagogues elsewhere in this encyclopedia (e.g., ipamorelin, CJC-1295, GHRP-6), somatropin supplies growth hormone directly rather than stimulating the pituitary to release its own.

Somatropin is produced via recombinant DNA technology (typically in E. coli or mammalian expression systems) and is structurally identical to the major isoform of endogenous human growth hormone: a 191-amino-acid, single-chain polypeptide with four cysteine residues forming two intrachain disulfide bonds. Multiple manufacturers market essentially identical or near-identical rhGH products under different brand names (Genotropin, Humatrope, Norditropin, Saizen, Nutropin, Omnitrope, Zomacton), with Serostim licensed specifically for HIV-associated wasting. It binds the growth hormone receptor (GHR), a class I cytokine receptor that dimerizes upon ligand binding and activates JAK2-STAT5 intracellular signaling, driving hepatic IGF-1 production and direct anabolic and metabolic effects across multiple tissues. Overview

Ipamorelin is a synthetic pentapeptide and selective agonist of the ghrelin / growth hormone secretagogue receptor (GHS-R). It stimulates pulsatile growth hormone (GH) release from the pituitary and is notably selective — it does not meaningfully raise ACTH, cortisol, or prolactin. It is not FDA-approved, is prohibited in sport, and reached only phase II trials before being discontinued for lack of efficacy in its tested indication.

Ipamorelin (development code NNC 26-0161) was originally developed by Novo Nordisk and is a pentapeptide with the sequence Aib-His-D-2-Nal-D-Phe-Lys-NH2, derived from the growth-hormone-releasing peptide GHRP-1. It contains non-standard amino acids (aminoisobutyric acid and D-2-naphthylalanine) that improve stability. Its defining pharmacological feature is selectivity: in animal studies it released GH with potency comparable to GHRP-6 but, unlike GHRP-2 and GHRP-6, did not increase ACTH or cortisol. It was investigated in phase II trials for postoperative ileus but discontinued for lack of efficacy. It is widely used non-clinically (often combined with a GHRH analog such as CJC-1295) to stimulate endogenous GH, but has no approved human therapeutic indication.

Mechanism of Action

Selective agonist at the ghrelin/growth hormone secretagogue receptor (GHS-R) on pituitary somatotrophs, stimulating pulsatile GH release. Acts via a GHRP-like receptor pathway distinct from GHRH, and is selective for GH release without significant effect on ACTH, cortisol, prolactin, FSH, LH, or TSH.

Overview

KPV is a tripeptide (Lys-Pro-Val) corresponding to the C-terminal sequence of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH). It is studied for anti-inflammatory effects, particularly in intestinal inflammation (inflammatory bowel disease models) and skin conditions, and can act both systemically and topically. It is not FDA-approved.

KPV is the C-terminal tripeptide of alpha-MSH and retains much of the parent hormone's anti-inflammatory activity without its pigmentary (melanocortin receptor) effects. Research, largely in cell and animal models, indicates KPV can enter cells directly and via the intestinal peptide transporter PepT1, where it down-modulates pro-inflammatory signaling (including NF-kappaB pathways). It has been investigated for inflammatory bowel disease and for inflammatory skin conditions such as eczema and psoriasis. Evidence is preclinical; it is among peptides under FDA 503A compounding review.

Acts intracellularly to inhibit pro-inflammatory signaling, including NF-kappaB activation and downstream inflammatory cytokine production. In the gut it is taken up by the peptide transporter PepT1 in intestinal epithelial cells, reducing mucosal inflammation. Overview

Mazdutide is a long-acting synthetic oxyntomodulin analog and dual agonist of the GLP-1 and glucagon receptors, co-developed by Innovent Biologics and Eli Lilly. It is approved as a prescription drug in China for weight management but remains investigational in the United States, with no FDA approval as of this review.

Mazdutide (IBI362 / LY3305677) is a synthetic peptide analog of oxyntomodulin, a naturally occurring gut hormone with dual activity at the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) and glucagon receptor (GCGR). Its peptide backbone incorporates a fatty-acyl modification that extends its in vivo half-life for once-weekly dosing. In published phase 3 Chinese trials, GLORY-1 (NEJM 2025) reported -12.55% body weight at 32 weeks with the 6 mg dose, and GLORY-2 (JAMA 2026) evaluated a 9 mg dose. A head-to-head phase 3 trial versus semaglutide 1 mg in early type 2 diabetes with obesity has also been conducted. Mazdutide has legal prescription status in China for weight management, making it one of the first drugs of its dual GLP-1/glucagon class to reach a regulatory market, but it remains investigational for the US market with no FDA approval. It is a distinct molecular entity from retatrutide (also Lilly-connected) and the two are not interchangeable; no head-to-head trial between them exists.

Mechanism of Action

Dual agonist at the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) and glucagon receptor (GCGR), mimicking the natural gut hormone oxyntomodulin. GLP-1R activity enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion, slows gastric emptying, and suppresses appetite; GCGR activity adds an energy-expenditure/thermogenic component not present in single GLP-1 agonists. Reported binding affinities: GCGR Ki of 17.7 nM (human) / 15.9 nM (mouse); GLP-1R Ki of 28.6 nM (human) / 25.1 nM (mouse); stimulates insulin secretion in mouse islets with an EC50 of 5.2 nM.

Overview

Melanotan II is a synthetic, non-selective melanocortin receptor agonist developed at the University of Arizona as a tanning agent. It activates MC1R, MC3R, MC4R, and MC5R with comparable affinity, producing skin pigmentation and, as an incidental finding in early trials, erectile/libido effects. It is not FDA-approved or approved by any regulatory agency for any use, and carries documented safety concerns distinct from its FDA-approved, more selective derivative bremelanotide (PT-141).

Melanotan II (Ac-Nle-cyclo[Asp-His-D-Phe-Arg-Trp-Lys]-NH2) is a cyclic heptapeptide analog of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), originally developed as a potential skin-cancer-prevention strategy by inducing protective tanning without UV exposure. Unlike native alpha-MSH, which preferentially activates MC1R on melanocytes, MT-2 is non-selective and activates MC1R, MC3R, MC4R, and MC5R with broadly comparable affinity. This non-selectivity is clinically significant: MC4R activation in the hypothalamus and spinal cord drives the erectile/libido effect that emerged as an unanticipated finding in the first human pilot trials (and was later developed separately into the FDA-approved, more selective drug bremelanotide/PT-141), while MC3R/MC5R activation contributes to appetite suppression and other autonomic effects. No government regulatory agency has approved any MT-2-containing product. Documented human harms include a published case report of eruptive atypical nevi and growth of pre-existing nevi in a patient with prior melanoma and dysplastic nevus syndrome (Cardones & Grichnik, 2009), plus other published reports of priapism requiring surgical intervention and rhabdomyolysis associated with self-administered use.

Non-selective agonist across the melanocortin receptor family (MC1R, MC3R, MC4R, MC5R). MC1R activation on melanocytes stimulates eumelanin synthesis (tanning). MC4R activation in the central nervous system drives sexual arousal/erectile activity and contributes to appetite suppression; MC3R/MC5R activation produces additional autonomic effects (cardiovascular tone, exocrine secretion).

Overview

MOTS-c is a 16-amino-acid mitochondrial-derived peptide encoded by the mitochondrial MT-RNR1 (12S rRNA) gene. It regulates metabolism — promoting glucose uptake and insulin sensitivity via the AMPK pathway — and is upregulated by exercise, leading to its description as an 'exercise mimetic.' It is studied for metabolic and aging-related applications but is not FDA-approved.

MOTS-c (sequence MRWQEMGYIFYPRKLR) is one of a small family of mitochondrial-derived peptides encoded within the mitochondrial 12S rRNA region; its first 11 residues are highly conserved across mammalian species. It has endocrine-like and nuclear transcriptional regulatory roles in muscle metabolism, insulin sensitivity, and body weight. In animal models it promotes metabolic homeostasis and reduces obesity and insulin resistance, and human cohort studies have linked lower circulating MOTS-c to adverse metabolic features (higher fasting insulin, HbA1c, BMI). Most therapeutic data are preclinical. It is among peptides under FDA 503A compounding review.

Promotes glucose uptake and metabolic homeostasis largely through activation of the AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) pathway, enhancing skeletal-muscle glucose metabolism and insulin sensitivity. Translocates to the nucleus under metabolic stress to regulate gene expression, giving it endocrine-like and transcriptional regulatory activity.

Overview

NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) is an essential coenzyme found in every living cell, required for cellular energy (ATP) production, DNA repair, and as a substrate for sirtuin enzymes involved in aging biology. It is not a peptide (it is a dinucleotide) but is widely marketed alongside peptides as an IV or subcutaneous infusion for energy, cognition, and anti-aging. It is not FDA-approved as a drug for any of these marketed indications; controlled human trial evidence for IV/injectable NAD+ specifically is limited.

NAD+ is composed of two nucleotides joined by a pyrophosphate bond: one bearing adenine, the other bearing nicotinamide. It exists in oxidized (NAD+) and reduced (NADH) forms and cycles between them as a central electron carrier in cellular respiration, making it essential for mitochondrial ATP production. Beyond energy metabolism, NAD+ is a required substrate for sirtuins (NAD-dependent deacetylases implicated in aging and metabolic regulation), PARP enzymes involved in DNA repair, and CD38, which consumes NAD+ and whose activity increases with age -- a proposed mechanism for the age-related decline in tissue NAD+ levels that underlies much of the 'NAD+ boosting' longevity marketing. Unlike its precursors nicotinamide riboside (NR) and nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), which are sold as oral supplements with a larger human trial base, direct IV or subcutaneous NAD+ administration has a much thinner controlled-trial evidence base; most published human data are small, short-term tolerability/pilot studies rather than large randomized efficacy trials for any of the commercially marketed benefits (energy, cognition, hangover recovery, anti-aging).

Mechanism of Action

Functions as a coenzyme carrying electrons in oxidation-reduction reactions central to mitochondrial ATP synthesis (glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation). Serves as an obligate substrate for sirtuin deacetylases, PARP DNA-repair enzymes, and NAD-glycohydrolases (e.g., CD38), linking cellular NAD+ availability to energy metabolism, genomic stability, and proposed aging pathways.

Overview

PEG-MGF is a pegylated (polyethylene-glycol-conjugated) version of Mechano Growth Factor (MGF), the C-terminal E-domain peptide of the IGF-1Ec splice variant that is naturally expressed within hours of mechanical muscle damage to activate satellite cells. Pegylation extends native MGF's half-life from minutes to hours-to-days. It has essentially no human clinical data and is not FDA-approved; the parent hormone IGF-1 (mecasermin) is separately FDA-approved for a specific pediatric deficiency indication, which should not be conflated with PEG-MGF itself.

MGF (Mechano Growth Factor) is the unique 24-amino-acid C-terminal E-domain peptide produced by alternative splicing of the IGF1 gene, first characterized by Geoffrey Goldspink's laboratory at University College London. Unlike the mature IGF-1 domain (which signals through IGF-1R and is associated with cell proliferation broadly, including in oncology contexts), the MGF E-domain has distinct, more localized biological activity: it is the first IGF-1 splice variant expressed after mechanical muscle damage (within 0-2 hours), peaking at 2-6 hours to activate quiescent satellite cells, before IGF-1Ea expression rises at 6-72 hours to drive differentiation and protein synthesis. Native MGF has an extremely short half-life of approximately 5-7 minutes, severely limiting its practical research utility; PEGylation -- attaching a polyethylene glycol polymer chain -- extends this to hours or days by shielding the peptide from proteolytic degradation and reducing renal clearance, at the cost of introducing a class-wide PEGylation risk: repeated dosing can induce anti-PEG antibodies leading to accelerated clearance on subsequent doses (the 'ABC phenomenon'). PEG-MGF remains entirely preclinical, with animal and cell-culture data on satellite cell activation, and separately-published research on neurogenesis and neuroprotection in brain injury/aging models via the same E-domain peptide. It has no human clinical trial data and is not FDA-approved for any indication.

Mechanism of Action

Activates quiescent muscle satellite cells (the resident stem-cell population responsible for muscle repair and hypertrophy), expanding the progenitor pool as the first-responding IGF-1 splice variant after mechanical damage. This is mechanistically distinct from mature IGF-1 signaling through IGF-1R (implicated more broadly in cell proliferation, including tumor growth pathways) and from myostatin-inhibition approaches (e.g., follistatin), which remove an anti-growth brake rather than actively recruiting progenitor cells. Separately studied for neurogenic and neuroprotective activity via the same E-domain peptide in brain injury/aging models.

Overview

PT-141 (bremelanotide) is an FDA-approved melanocortin receptor agonist marketed as Vyleesi for acquired, generalized hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD) in premenopausal women. It acts through central (brain) arousal pathways rather than the vascular system, distinguishing it from erectile-dysfunction drugs. It is a subcutaneous injection taken before anticipated sexual activity.

Bremelanotide is a cyclic heptapeptide derived from melanotan II. It was approved by the FDA in June 2019 (Vyleesi) for acquired, generalized HSDD in premenopausal women. It activates melanocortin receptors (notably MC4R) in the central nervous system; the precise mechanism by which it improves sexual desire is not fully established. The approved product is a subcutaneous autoinjector delivering 1.75 mg, used at least 45 minutes before anticipated sexual activity, with no more than one dose per 24 hours and no more than eight per month. It can cause a transient increase in blood pressure and decrease in heart rate, and is associated with focal hyperpigmentation. Although the approved indication is for women, it is also used off-label and sold by research-chemical vendors for other purposes; only the Vyleesi indication is FDA-approved.

Mechanism of Action

Agonist at melanocortin receptors (including MC4R) in the central nervous system, modulating neural pathways involved in sexual desire and arousal. Unlike PDE5 inhibitors, it works centrally rather than through peripheral vascular effects. The exact mechanism for its effect on desire is not fully characterized.

Overview

Retatrutide is an investigational triple hormone receptor agonist, developed by Eli Lilly, that simultaneously activates the GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon receptors. It produced the largest pharmacological weight loss recorded to date in a phase 2 trial (24.2% at 48 weeks). It is NOT yet FDA-approved -- it remains in phase 3 (the TRIUMPH program) as of this review, and claims of approval circulating in some vendor/marketing material are inaccurate.

Retatrutide (LY3437943) is a synthetic ~39-amino-acid peptide built on a GIP receptor agonist backbone, engineered to also activate the GLP-1 and glucagon receptors, making it the first-in-class 'triple G' (GIP/GLP-1/glucagon) agonist. It binds human GCGR, GIPR, and GLP-1R with reported EC50 values of 5.79, 0.0643, and 0.775 nM respectively. Unlike dual GIP/GLP-1 agonists such as tirzepatide, the added glucagon receptor activity contributes a thermogenic and energy-expenditure component: despite glucagon receptor activation normally raising blood glucose, retatrutide produces net glucose lowering because the GLP-1 and GIP effects predominate. A phase 2 trial (NEJM 2023) reported up to 24.2% mean body weight loss at 48 weeks (12 mg dose) -- the most substantial pharmacological weight loss recorded to date, with weight curves still declining at study end; newer 68-week data have reported up to 28.7% loss at the highest dose. As of this review, retatrutide is still completing phase 3 trials (the TRIUMPH program) and has NOT received FDA approval; some vendor/marketing sources inaccurately state it is FDA-approved, which should be disregarded.

Mechanism of Action

Simultaneous agonist at three G-protein-coupled receptors: the glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor (GIPR), the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R), and the glucagon receptor (GCGR). GLP-1R activity slows gastric emptying, enhances satiety, and reduces appetite; GIPR activity enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion and supports beta-cell function; GCGR activity adds a thermogenic, energy-expenditure-raising component not present in dual GIP/GLP-1 agonists. The combined GLP-1/GIP insulinotropic effect outweighs glucagon's glucose-raising tendency, producing net glucose lowering.

Semaglutide is an FDA-approved glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist used to treat type 2 diabetes (Ozempic, Rybelsus) and for chronic weight management (Wegovy), with additional approved indications including reduction of major adverse cardiovascular events. It is a once-weekly injectable (also available as an oral tablet) with a half-life of about one week.

It carries a boxed warning regarding rodent thyroid C-cell tumors and is contraindicated in patients with a personal/family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2.

Selective GLP-1 receptor agonist. It enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppresses glucagon, slows gastric emptying, and acts on appetite-regulating areas of the brain to reduce food intake. The glucose-dependence of its insulinotropic effect limits hypoglycemia risk when used alone.

Semax is a synthetic heptapeptide analog of the ACTH(4-10) fragment, developed at the Institute of Molecular Genetics of the Russian Academy of Sciences. It is studied as a neuroprotective nootropic that upregulates the neurotrophins BDNF and NGF without stimulating cortisol. It is used clinically in Russia for some neurological indications but is not FDA-approved in the United States.

Semax has the sequence Met-Glu-His-Phe-Pro-Gly-Pro (MEHFPGP), built by appending a C-terminal Pro-Gly-Pro tripeptide to the ACTH(4-7) fragment to resist enzymatic degradation. Unlike full ACTH, it does not stimulate cortisol release. Preclinical and Russian clinical research has examined it for cognitive enhancement, stroke/ischemia neuroprotection, and attention, with proposed mechanisms centered on rapid upregulation of BDNF and its receptor TrkB in the hippocampus, modulation of nitric oxide and lipid peroxidation, and effects on monoaminergic signaling. In the U.S. it is sold as a research chemical (often as the more stable N-acetyl amidated derivative) and is among peptides under FDA 503A compounding review.

Mechanism of Action

Proposed to rapidly increase expression of BDNF and TrkB in the hippocampus, support neurotrophic/neuroprotective signaling, regulate cortical nitric oxide and lipid peroxidation, and modulate monoamine neurotransmitter systems. As an ACTH(4-10) analog it retains neurotropic activity without the corticotropic (cortisol-releasing) effect of full ACTH.

Overview

SS-31 (elamipretide) is a mitochondria-targeted tetrapeptide that binds and stabilizes cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane, improving mitochondrial function and reducing reactive oxygen species. It is an investigational drug (developed by Stealth BioTherapeutics) studied in mitochondrial diseases such as Barth syndrome, mitochondrial myopathy, and Friedreich's ataxia, as well as dry age-related macular degeneration. It is not FDA-approved.

SS-31 (elamipretide; development codes MTP-131, Bendavia) is a small aromatic-cationic tetrapeptide, D-Arg-Dmt-Lys-Phe-NH2 (where Dmt is 2,6-dimethyltyrosine), with limited blood-brain-barrier penetration. It concentrates in the inner mitochondrial membrane and binds cardiolipin, stabilizing membrane structure and the electron transport chain, thereby improving mitochondrial energetics and reducing toxic reactive oxygen species. In animal and cellular models it has reversed mitochondrial fragmentation and markers of disease in mitochondrial cardiomyopathies, Friedreich's ataxia, Barth syndrome, and ischemia-reperfusion injury, and it also suppresses macrophage activation and inflammasome signaling. It has been generally well tolerated in clinical trials with preliminary signs of benefit, but it remains investigational and is not FDA-approved.

Mechanism of Action

Concentrates in the inner mitochondrial membrane and binds cardiolipin, stabilizing membrane architecture and the electron transport chain. This improves mitochondrial respiration and ATP production and reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS). Secondary anti-inflammatory effects include suppression of the Nrf2-dependent NLRP3 inflammasome and M1 macrophage polarization via ROS scavenging.

Overview

TB-500 is a synthetic, N-acetylated heptapeptide (Ac-LKKTETQ) corresponding to the actin-binding fragment (residues 17-23) of thymosin beta-4 (Tβ4), a naturally occurring 43-amino-acid peptide involved in tissue repair, cell migration, and angiogenesis. It is frequently marketed as 'Thymosin Beta-4,' but the two are not identical. TB-500 is not FDA-approved, is prohibited in sport, and has no completed human efficacy trials as of 2026.

There is an important distinction often blurred in the marketplace: full-length thymosin beta-4 (Tβ4) is a 43-amino-acid endogenous peptide (CAS 77591-33-4, MW ~4963 Da) that is among the most abundant G-actin-sequestering molecules in mammalian cells and has a substantial independent research literature, including cardiac-repair and wound-healing work. 'TB-500' as sold by research-chemical vendors is typically the much smaller synthetic heptapeptide Ac-LKKTETQ (CAS 885340-08-9, MW ~878 Da), the N-acetylated active actin-binding fragment. Most of the strong basic science (cardiac regeneration, corneal/dermal wound healing) was conducted on full-length Tβ4 or its pharmaceutical formulation (RGN-259), not on the LKKTETQ fragment specifically. Evidence for systemic injectable TB-500 in musculoskeletal injury is preclinical and anecdotal; no completed randomized controlled trials exist for that use as of 2026. TB-500 is commonly stacked with BPC-157 (informally the 'Wolverine stack'), again without controlled human data.

Mechanism of Action

The parent peptide thymosin beta-4 acts primarily by sequestering globular (G-)actin, modulating actin dynamics, cell migration, angiogenesis, and inflammation. In cardiac models, Tβ4 forms a complex with PINCH and integrin-linked kinase (ILK), activating the survival kinase Akt and promoting cardiomyocyte survival and migration. The LKKTETQ fragment (TB-500) corresponds to the actin-binding site and is proposed to retain much of this actin-related activity, though fragment-specific mechanistic data are more limited than for the full peptide.

Overview

Tesamorelin is an FDA-approved synthetic analog of the full 44-amino-acid growth-hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH), marketed as Egrifta. It is approved specifically to reduce excess visceral abdominal fat in HIV-infected adults with lipodystrophy. Unlike exogenous growth hormone, it stimulates the pituitary's own pulsatile GH release via the GHRH receptor.

Tesamorelin is GHRH(1-44) modified with a trans-3-hexenoic acid group at the N-terminal tyrosine, which confers resistance to DPP-IV enzymatic degradation and extends its short native half-life. It was FDA-approved in November 2010 (Egrifta) for reduction of excess abdominal fat in HIV-positive adults with lipodystrophy, based on a pivotal phase III trial (Falutz et al., NEJM 2007, n=412) showing a 15.2% reduction in visceral adipose tissue, an 81% increase in IGF-1, and improvements in triglycerides and cholesterol ratio at 26 weeks. Newer formulations (Egrifta SV, approved 2019; Egrifta WR) reduce injection volume and reconstitution frequency but are not interchangeable milligram-for-milligram with the original formulation. It selectively reduces visceral fat with little effect on subcutaneous fat or body weight, and its effect reverses if treatment is stopped.

Mechanism of Action

Binds the GHRH receptor (GHRHR) on pituitary somatotrophs, activating the Gs-alpha/adenylate cyclase/cAMP pathway to stimulate pulsatile GH synthesis and release. This raises hepatic IGF-1 production, which drives preferential lipolysis of visceral adipose tissue.

Overview

Thymosin Alpha-1 (INN thymalfasin) is a 28-amino-acid thymic peptide and immune modulator. It is approved in more than 30-35 countries under the brand name Zadaxin for chronic hepatitis B (and used for hepatitis C, certain cancers, and as an immune adjunct), but it is NOT FDA-approved in the United States. In the US it holds 503A Category 2 status, available by prescription through licensed compounding pharmacies in some states.

Thymosin Alpha-1 was the first peptide isolated from thymic tissue (thymosin fraction 5) and is the N-terminal acetylated 28-amino-acid cleavage product of prothymosin alpha. Its sequence is highly conserved across species. It is generally well tolerated, with injection-site reactions the most common adverse effect.

Activates toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9) signaling on dendritic and other immune cells, promoting Th1 polarization, maturation of T cells, increased NK-cell activity, and enhanced interferon production and antibody responses to T-cell-dependent antigens.

Overview

Tirzepatide is an FDA-approved dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist, the first medication to activate both incretin receptors. It is approved for type 2 diabetes (Mounjaro) and chronic weight management and obstructive sleep apnea in obesity (Zepbound). It is a once-weekly subcutaneous injection with a half-life of about 5 days and has shown greater weight loss than selective GLP-1 agonists in trials.

Tirzepatide is a 39-amino-acid modified peptide based on the GIP sequence, containing two non-coded aminoisobutyric acid (Aib) residues (positions 2 and 13), a C-terminal amide, and a Lys at position 20 attached to a C20 fatty diacid (1,20-eicosanedioic acid) via a linker that enables albumin binding and prolongs half-life. It was FDA-approved on May 13, 2022 (Mounjaro) for type 2 diabetes, the first and only GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist for that indication, and on November 8, 2023 (Zepbound) for chronic weight management; Zepbound is also approved for moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity. Like semaglutide, it is a fully approved prescription drug with extensive clinical trial data and carries a boxed warning regarding rodent thyroid C-cell tumors.

Mechanism of Action

Dual agonist at the GIP and GLP-1 receptors. It enhances first- and second-phase glucose-dependent insulin secretion, reduces glucagon, slows gastric emptying, and decreases food intake via appetite-regulating pathways. The addition of GIP activity is proposed to further augment effects on food intake and metabolism beyond GLP-1 alone.

Proposed complementary mechanisms (TB-500 via actin sequestration; BPC-157 via NO/angiogenesis pathways). Combination is popular anecdotally but unsupported by controlled human data.
